terms.core_definition: Construct Adequacy is a foundational psychometric and research design concept articulated by Donald P. Schwab (1980) that evaluates the fidelity, correspondence, and operational soundness of the linkage between an abstract, unobservable theoretical construct and its concrete empirical operationalization (measurement instrument or experimental manipulation). Schwab demonstrated that organizational and social science research is frequently compromised by treating operational measures as perfect reflections of constructs, establishing that rigorous scientific inference requires demonstrating both construct adequacy (measurement validation) and substantive substantive relationship testing as distinct, mandatory research phases.
terms.seminal_citation: Schwab, D. P. (1980). Construct validity in organizational behavior. In B. M. Staw & L. L. Cummings (Eds.), Research in organizational behavior (Vol. 2, pp. 3-43). JAI Press.
terms.expert_notes: Đã được biên tập và chuẩn hóa định nghĩa học thuật theo giáo trình kinh điển.
terms.core_definition_en: Rigorous scholarly definition of Construct adequacy according to established research methodology literature.
terms.operational_mechanism:
Evaluating construct adequacy requires assessing three fundamental correspondence zones:
1. Construct Deficiency: Occurs when the empirical measure fails to capture important theoretical dimensions of the underlying construct (under-representation, e.g., measuring Job Performance solely through punctuality).
2. Construct Contamination: Occurs when the empirical measure inadvertently captures irrelevant variance belonging to outside constructs or method artifacts (e.g., measuring Intelligence through a test requiring heavy cultural familiarity or English fluency).
3. Valid Construct Overlap: The true intersection where the operational measure faithfully and exclusively reflects the target theoretical construct.
4. Dual-Phase Research Program: Schwab's mandate that researchers must formally establish measurement adequacy (via CFA, AVE, reliability, and discriminant testing) *before* testing substantive hypothesized relationships among constructs.
terms.benchmarks:
Methodological standards (Schwab, 1980; MacKenzie, Podsakoff, & Podsakoff, 2011):
- Two-Step Modeling Mandate (Anderson & Gerbing, 1988): Estimating and achieving satisfactory fit for the confirmatory measurement model before evaluating the structural regression model.
- Variance Explained Threshold: A construct-adequate measure should demonstrate that latent constructs explain $> 50\%$ of indicator variance ($\text{AVE} \ge 0.50$).
- Content Domain Mapping: Establishing that items comprehensively cover the theoretical conceptual definition without leaving major sub-facets unmeasured.
terms.pitfalls:
Common research design defects in top-tier journal submissions:
1. Conflating Measurement Validation with Hypothesis Testing: Estimating measurement and structural models simultaneously in a single step, concealing serious measurement inadequacies behind apparent structural path significance.
2. Severe Construct Contamination: Utilizing self-report measures that embed confounding personality traits (e.g., measuring 'Work Stress' with items that capture general 'Negative Affectivity').
3. Single-Item Measure Deficiency: Using single-item indicators to measure broad, multifaceted psychological or strategic constructs (e.g., measuring 'Firm Innovation' with a single question), guaranteeing severe construct deficiency.
terms.apa_reference: MacKenzie, S. B., Podsakoff, P. M., & Podsakoff, N. P. (2011). Construct measurement and validation procedures in MIS and behavioral research: Integrating new and existing techniques. MIS Quarterly, 35(2), 293-334. https://doi.org/10.2307/23044045

terms.core_definition: Construct Intension vs. Extension is a fundamental epistemological and taxonomic principle of concept formation, formalized in social science by Giovanni Sartori (1970) in his classic 'Ladder of Abstraction' and updated for management scholarship by Philip M. Podsakoff, Scott B. MacKenzie, and Nathan P. Podsakoff (2016). Construct Intension (connotation) refers to the internal defining properties, essential attributes, and boundaries that constitute the core meaning of a concept. Construct Extension (denotation) refers to the universe of empirical entities, cases, or classes of objects in the real world to which that concept applies. In formal logic and concept design, intension and extension are inversely related: as a researcher adds defining attributes to a concept's intension (making it richer and more specific), its empirical extension narrows.
terms.seminal_citation: Sartori, G. (1970). Concept misformation in comparative politics. The American Political Science Review, 64(4), 1033-1053. https://doi.org/10.2307/1958356
terms.expert_notes: Đã chuẩn hóa từ bảng trích xuất sang định dạng từ điển chuẩn.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Construct intension vs extension according to MacKenzie et al. (2011).
terms.operational_mechanism:
Sartori's Ladder of Abstraction operates across three taxonomic levels:
1. High-Level Abstraction (Universal Concepts): Minimal intension (few defining attributes) and maximal extension (applies to vast populations across time and space, e.g., 'Organization', 'Social Group').
2. Medium-Level Abstraction (Taxonomic Typologies): Balanced intension and extension; specific sub-categories with bounded empirical reach (e.g., 'Bureaucratic Hospital', 'Tech Startup').
3. Low-Level Abstraction (Contextualized Substantive Concepts): Rich, complex intension (many explicit defining criteria) and narrow, highly specific extension (e.g., 'Venture-backed Series A Fintech Startup in Southeast Asia').
4. Inverse Variation Law: Expanding the empirical applicability of a concept without appropriately stripping away specific defining attributes results in conceptual stretching, a severe methodological error.
terms.benchmarks:
Concept formation benchmarks (Sartori, 1970; Podsakoff et al., 2016):
- Clear Intensional Definition: A research manuscript must provide a formal, explicit conceptual definition specifying: (a) the overarching conceptual category (genus), and (b) the distinguishing unique characteristics (differentia specifica).
- Boundary Condition Specification: The author must explicitly delineate the extensional domain of applicability—clarifying not only where the construct applies, but where it ceases to apply.
- Mutual Exclusivity: Sub-categories across the ladder of abstraction must maintain clear boundary demarcations.
terms.pitfalls:
Critical concept formation traps in top journals:
1. Conceptual Stretching (Conceptual Straining): Taking a concept formulated in one specific context (e.g., 'Transformational Leadership' developed in Western corporate boardrooms) and stretching it to apply universally across radical, distinct settings (e.g., informal guerrilla networks) without adjusting its intensional properties.
2. Intensional Vagueness: Defining a construct with ambiguous, poetic, or circular language, making it impossible to determine which empirical entities fall into its extension.
3. The 'Everything and Nothing' Trap: Defining a concept so broadly that its extension covers all human behavior, rendering the construct analytically useless.
terms.apa_reference: Podsakoff, P. M., MacKenzie, S. B., & Podsakoff, N. P. (2016). Recommendations for creating better concept definitions in the organizational, behavioral, and social sciences. Organizational Research Methods, 19(2), 159-203. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094428115624965

terms.term: Construct Scores (Latent Factor Scores vs. Summed Scores)
terms.vietnamese: Điểm số cấu trúc (Điểm nhân tố tiềm ẩn so với Điểm tổng cộng)
terms.core_definition: Construct Scores refer to the operational numerical values assigned to individual respondents to represent their standing on an unobservable latent construct, derived either through coarse Summed Scores (averaging or adding item ratings) or through statistical Factor Scores (model-based latent estimates). Analyzed comprehensively by Christine DiStefano, Min Zhu, and Diana Mindrila (2009), factor scores use factor loadings and error uniquenesses from Exploratory or Confirmatory Factor Analysis to weight indicators optimally (via Regression, Bartlett, or Anderson-Rubin methods), whereas summed scores treat all indicators as essentially parallel with equal unit weights.
terms.seminal_citation: DiStefano, C., Zhu, M., & Mindrila, D. (2009). Understanding and using factor scores: Considerations for the applied researcher. Practical Assessment, Research, and Evaluation, 14, Article 20. https://doi.org/10.7275/da8t-4g52
terms.expert_notes: Lộ tên file nội bộ
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Construct scores according to Henseler et al. (2015); Henseler et al. (2015).
terms.operational_mechanism:
The comparative estimation methods function as follows:
1. Non-Refined Summed Scores: Simple arithmetic sum or mean: $S_i = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^k X_{ij}$. Assumes items are strictly tau-equivalent with identical measurement error; easy to compute and interpret across lay audiences.
2. Refined Factor Scores (Regression Method - Thurstone):
$$\hat{\mathbf{F}} = \mathbf{R}_{FF} \mathbf{\Lambda}^T \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{X}$$
Maximizes determinacy and correlation between estimated and true factor scores, but yields biased (non-orthogonal) scores for orthogonal factors.
3. Bartlett Predictor: Weighted least squares method that minimizes unique factor variance, producing unbiased factor estimates ($\mathbb{E}[\hat{F}] = F$).
4. Anderson-Rubin Method: An orthogonal modification of Bartlett scores guaranteeing that factor scores are strictly uncorrelated, ideal for subsequent multicollinearity-free OLS regressions.
5. Factor Indeterminacy Problem: Because common factor models have more latent variables (common + unique) than observed variables, an infinite number of factor score sets can produce the exact same observed covariance matrix.
terms.benchmarks:
Methodological criteria (DiStefano et al., 2009; Hair et al., 2019):
- Factor Determinacy: The correlation between true and estimated factor scores ($ho$) must be $\ge 0.80$ (and preferably $\ge 0.90$) for factor scores to be validly used in subsequent statistical analyses.
- High-Loading Homogeneity: When factor loadings are uniformly high ($\lambda_i > 0.75$) and approximately equal, summed scores correlate at $r > 0.95$ with Bartlett factor scores, rendering summed scores practically equivalent.
- Latent Variable SEM Superiority: Full structural equation modeling (SEM) that estimates structural paths concurrently with the measurement model without extracting intermediate factor scores is superior, eliminating measurement error attenuation entirely.
terms.pitfalls:
Common analytical flaws in empirical submissions:
1. The Two-Step Factor Score Fallacy: Extracting factor scores from CFA and treating them as 'observed error-free variables' in subsequent OLS regressions, ignoring the standard error of factor score estimation and biasing downstream standard errors.
2. Using Unit Sums on Incommensurate Scales: Summing raw items without standardization when items were measured on different response scales (e.g., combining a 5-point Likert item with a 100-point scale).
3. Retaining Low-Quality Items in Sums: Averaging items with factor loadings $< 0.40$ into a composite score, diluting true construct variance with random noise.
terms.apa_reference: Grice, J. W. (2001). Computing and evaluating factor scores. Psychological Methods, 6(4), 430-450. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.6.4.430

terms.core_definition: Construct Validity in the landmark methodological framework of William R. Shadish, Thomas D. Cook, and Donald T. Campbell (2002)—widely designated as the SCC Framework—is one of the four foundational validity types in generalized causal inference (alongside Statistical Conclusion Validity, Internal Validity, and External Validity). It evaluates the degree to which inferences can be legitimately made from the operational study instances (the specific sampling, experimental manipulations, measurement instruments, and operational settings implemented) to the higher-order theoretical constructs they represent, ensuring that the study truly tests the theoretical concepts intended rather than alternative, unintended constructs.
terms.seminal_citation: Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for generalized causal inference. Houghton Mifflin.
terms.expert_notes: Trùng #529, #530; rác Markdown/bảng; mảnh trích
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Construct Validity (SCC) according to Shadish, Cook & Campbell (2002).
terms.operational_mechanism:
The SCC construct validity evaluation requires assessing explicit operational threats:
1. Inadequate Explication of Constructs: Formulating vague theoretical definitions, leading to operationalizations that fail to capture essential construct properties.
2. Construct Confounding: An operational manipulation or measure simultaneously embodies two distinct theoretical constructs (e.g., an intervention designed to test 'peer mentoring' inadvertently introduces 'authoritarian supervision').
3. Mono-Operation Bias: Using only a single operationalization of the independent or dependent variable, which under-represents construct complexity and confounds the construct with specific method artifacts.
4. Mono-Method Bias: Presenting all operationalizations through a single measurement modality (e.g., self-report questionnaires), inflating observed covariances.
5. Reactivity Threats to Construct Validity:
   - Hypothesis Guessing: Participants inferring the study purpose and altering behavior.
   - Evaluation Apprehension: Anxiety about being judged causing unnatural performance.
   - Experimenter Expectancies: Subtle cues from investigators biasing subject responses.
terms.benchmarks:
Design benchmarks in experimental and quasi-experimental studies (Shadish et al., 2002):
- Multi-Operation / Multi-Method Design: Utilizing multiple distinct manipulations of the independent variable and multi-source dependent measures (e.g., self-report, behavioral observation, physiological tracking).
- Active Manipulation Checks: Incorporating independent checks to empirically verify that the experimental intervention successfully activated the intended psychological construct without inadvertently activating confounding constructs.
- Double-Blind Controls: Concealing conditions from both participants and experimenters to neutralize expectancy and hypothesis-guessing threats.
terms.pitfalls:
Common research design defects identified by reviewers:
1. Conflating Construct Validity with Internal Validity: Internal validity asks *whether* $A$ caused $B$; construct validity asks *what higher-order constructs* $A$ and $B$ represent. A study can possess perfect internal validity (proving an intervention worked) while possessing zero construct validity (completely misinterpreting what psychological mechanism was manipulated).
2. Relying on Single-Item Manipulations: Operationalizing a complex management intervention through a 1-sentence prompt, guaranteeing severe mono-operation bias.
3. Ignoring Participant Reactivity: Conducting laboratory experiments where subjects clearly guess the experimenter's hypothesis within 30 seconds, mistaking artificial demand compliance for authentic human behavior.
terms.apa_reference: Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (1979). Quasi-experimentation: Design & analysis issues for field settings. Rand McNally.

terms.core_definition: Constructivism—rooted in the cognitive developmental theories of Jean Piaget and Lev Vygotsky (1978) and formalized into social epistemology by Kenneth J. Gergen (1985)—is a philosophical and meta-theoretical paradigm asserting that human knowledge, social reality, and scientific categories are not passive reflections of an objective external universe waiting to be discovered, but are actively constructed through human cognition, social interactions, linguistic discourse, and cultural practices. Opposing naive positivism and direct realism, constructivism posits that reality is multiple, socially negotiated, and historically situated.
terms.seminal_citation: Vygotsky, L. S. (1978). Mind in society: The development of higher psychological processes. Harvard University Press.
terms.expert_notes: Đã được biên tập và chuẩn hóa định nghĩa học thuật theo giáo trình kinh điển.
terms.core_definition_en: Rigorous scholarly definition of Constructivism according to established research methodology literature.
terms.operational_mechanism:
Constructivism structures empirical inquiry through four operational commitments:
1. Relativist / Transactional Ontology: Reality is multiple, socially constructed, and context-dependent rather than a single, universal, static truth.
2. Subjectivist / Epistemological Co-Creation: The researcher and the researched are interactively linked; knowledge is co-constructed through ongoing dialogue rather than gathered by an objective, detached observer.
3. Hermeneutical and Dialectical Methodology: Employs interpretive, qualitative methods (in-depth interviews, ethnography, discourse analysis) to reconstruct and compare the varied subjective constructions that individuals hold.
4. Discursive Deconstruction: Analyzing how linguistic categories, metaphors, and institutional conventions actively generate social institutions (e.g., gender roles, organizational hierarchies, national identity).
terms.benchmarks:
Epistemological and methodological standards (Gergen, 1985; Lincoln & Guba, 1985):
- Reflexivity Requirement: The researcher must explicitly account for their own cultural, political, and theoretical positionality in shaping the interpretations.
- Plurality of Voices: Research outputs must present multiple competing perspectives and marginalized narratives rather than forcing a single consensus account.
- Audit Trail Rigor: Constructivist inquiries establish trustworthiness through credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability.
terms.pitfalls:
Common philosophical errors in empirical manuscripts:
1. Slipping into Radical Solipsism: Arguing that because reality is socially constructed, physical material facts (e.g., viruses, climate change, physical bullets) have no real existence outside of language (combated by Social Construction of Reality or Critical Realism).
2. The 'Anything Goes' Nihilism: Claiming that all constructions are equally valid, thereby abdicating the scientific responsibility to provide rigorous empirical evidence, audit trails, and coherent argumentation.
3. Using Positivist Quality Language: Stating that a constructivist study 'tested causal hypotheses and proved internal validity', which reflects complete paradigm confusion.
terms.apa_reference: Gergen, K. J. (1985). The social constructionist movement in modern psychology. American Psychologist, 40(3), 266-275. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.40.3.266

terms.core_definition: The Constructivism / Interpretivism Research Paradigm—comprehensively articulated in qualitative philosophy by Egon G. Guba and Yvonna S. Lincoln (1994) and Thomas A. Schwandt (1994)—is a foundational qualitative research paradigm that unites constructivist ontology (multiple, mind-dependent, socially constructed realities) with interpretivist epistemology (knowledge derived through the empathetic understanding—Verstehen—of subjective human experiences). Rejecting the positivist search for universal, time-free causal laws, the constructivist-interpretivist paradigm seeks to illuminate the nuanced, culturally contextualized meanings, values, and interpretive frameworks that human actors use to make sense of their lived worlds.
terms.seminal_citation: Guba, E. G., & Lincoln, Y. S. (1994). Competing paradigms in qualitative research. In N. K. Denzin & Y. S. Lincoln (Eds.), Handbook of qualitative research (pp. 105-117). SAGE Publications.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Constructivism / Interpretivism according to Guba & Lincoln (1994).
terms.operational_mechanism:
The paradigm operates through three interlocking philosophical axioms:
1. Relativist Ontology: Rejects a single objective reality; posits that multiple, socially constructed realities exist, each bounded by historical culture, language, and shared practices.
2. Subjectivist / Interactive Epistemology: Denies the possibility of a neutral, detached observer. The investigator and the participant are intimately engaged in a relational, transactional process of co-creating understanding.
3. Hermeneutic-Dialectical Methodology: Employs iterative, emergent qualitative designs where individual constructions are elicited and compared through hermeneutic analysis, moving between the parts and the whole (the hermeneutic circle) until a sophisticated, consensual reconstruction is achieved.
4. Inductive Theory Emergence: Generates theoretical propositions inductively from contextual narrative data rather than deducing hypotheses from abstract formal models.
terms.benchmarks:
Paradigm alignment benchmarks (Guba & Lincoln, 1994; Schwandt, 1994):
- Verstehen (Empathetic Understanding): Demonstrating that the analysis captures the internal subjective logic of participants from the 'emic' (insider) perspective.
- Naturalistic Contextualization: Data must be collected in natural, real-world field settings (workplaces, communities) without artificial experimental manipulation.
- Trustworthiness Framework: Evaluated via Lincoln and Guba's four-dimension criteria (Credibility, Transferability, Dependability, Confirmability) rather than positivist metrics (Internal Validity, External Validity, Reliability, Objectivity).
terms.pitfalls:
Common paradigm confusion in doctoral dissertations:
1. Epistemic Contradiction (Positivist Creep): Claiming to adopt an interpretivist paradigm while formulating statistical null hypotheses, using structured closed-ended surveys, and calculating $p$-values.
2. Superficial Descriptive Reporting: Reporting verbatim participant quotes without providing deep, contextual, and hermeneutic interpretation of the underlying cultural meanings.
3. Disregarding Transferability: Making sweeping claims of universal global generalizability, forgetting that interpretivist findings are bounded by the specific historical and sociocultural context investigated.
terms.apa_reference: Schwandt, T. A. (1994). Constructivist, interpretivist approaches to human inquiry. In N. K. Denzin & Y. S. Lincoln (Eds.), Handbook of qualitative research (pp. 118-137). SAGE Publications.

terms.vietnamese: Lý thuyết nền kiến tạo / Tiếp cận kiến tạo luận Kathy Charmaz

terms.core_definition: Constructivist Grounded Theory là bước tiến đương đại nổi bật nhất trong lý thuyết nền do Kathy Charmaz khởi xướng (2000, 2006, 2014), đặt trên nền tảng bản thể luận tương đối (relativist ontology) và nhận thức luận kiến tạo (constructivist epistemology). Charmaz bác bỏ giả định thực chứng ngầm định của Glaser và Strauss (cho rằng dữ liệu và lý thuyết tồn tại khách quan ngoài kia chỉ chờ nghiên cứu viên 'khám phá'). Ngược lại, bà khẳng định rằng cả dữ liệu lẫn lý thuyết đều là sản phẩm được 'đồng kiến tạo' (co-constructed) thông qua sự tương tác xã hội giữa nghiên cứu viên và người tham gia.
terms.seminal_citation: Charmaz, K. (2006). Constructing Grounded Theory: A Practical Guide Through Qualitative Analysis. SAGE Publications; Charmaz, K. (2014). Constructing Grounded Theory (2nd ed.). SAGE Publications.
terms.expert_notes: Đã được biên tập và chuẩn hóa định nghĩa học thuật theo giáo trình kinh điển.
terms.core_definition_en: Rigorous scholarly definition of Constructivist grounded theory according to established research methodology literature.
terms.operational_mechanism: Quy trình thực thi theo Charmaz: (1) Initial Coding: Mã hóa ban đầu sát từng dòng dữ liệu (line-by-line coding) bằng việc sử dụng các danh động từ chỉ hành động (gerunds - từ có đuôi '-ing') để nắm bắt tính linh động và tiến trình của trải nghiệm; (2) Focused Coding: Lựa chọn các mã xuất hiện thường xuyên nhất hoặc có ý nghĩa lý thuyết nhất để sàng lọc khối dữ liệu lớn; (3) Memo Writing: Viết bản ghi tự sự kết hợp phản tư cá nhân về vị thế nghiên cứu (reflexivity); (4) Theoretical Sampling & Saturation; (5) Xây dựng lý thuyết trừu tượng nhưng bám rễ sâu sắc vào bối cảnh văn hóa xã hội đa chiều.
benchmarks: Nguyên tắc mã hóa bằng hành động (Action/Gerund Coding): Sử dụng các động từ hành động (ví dụ: 'đàm phán vị thế', 'chống đỡ áp lực') thay vì các danh từ tĩnh tại.
Tính phản tư triệt để (Deep Reflexivity): Nhà nghiên cứu phải công khai vị thế quyền lực, cảm xúc và giả định cá nhân trong suốt tiến trình đồng kiến tạo tri thức.
Tôn trọng tiếng nói của người tham gia: Bản lý thuyết hoàn thiện phải chứa đựng các sắc thái cảm xúc, sự mâu thuẫn và tính đa thanh (polyvocality) của trải nghiệm sống.
pitfalls: Mã hóa thụ động bằng danh từ nhãn dán (static labeling): Dùng các danh từ tĩnh đóng hộp đối tượng thay vì nắm bắt hành động chuyển biến qua danh động từ.
Tuyên bố đạt chân lý khách quan tuyệt đối: Bỏ quên vị thế đồng kiến tạo, viết báo cáo theo giọng văn thực chứng xa cách ('nhà nghiên cứu đứng ngoài quan sát').
Biến tướng thành văn phong phê bình thuần túy: Sa đà vào cảm xúc cá nhân của nghiên cứu viên mà làm mờ nhạt câu chuyện và bằng chứng thực tế từ người tham gia.
terms.apa_reference: Charmaz, K. (2014). Constructing grounded theory (2nd ed.). SAGE Publications, Inc.

Lý thuyết nền kiến tạo của Kathy Charmaz
terms.core_definition: Constructivist Grounded Theory is an influential, contemporary qualitative methodology developed by Kathy Charmaz (2000, 2006, 2014) that repositions the classic grounded theory of Glaser and Strauss into a 21st-century constructivist, interpretivist, and reflexive framework. Rejecting the traditional objectivist, post-positivist assumption that theories reside 'out there' in the data waiting to be neutrally discovered by an objective scientist, Charmaz posits that both data and theories are actively constructed through the shared interactions, emotional dynamics, and linguistic relationships between the researcher and the participants.
terms.seminal_citation: Charmaz, K. (2000). Grounded theory: Objectivist and constructivist methods. In N. K. Denzin & Y. S. Lincoln (Eds.), Handbook of qualitative research (2nd ed., pp. 509-535). SAGE Publications.
terms.expert_notes: Trùng #534
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Constructivist Grounded Theory (Charmaz) according to Charmaz (2006/2014).
terms.operational_mechanism:
Charmaz's methodology operates through distinctive analytical practices:
1. Initial Coding with Gerunds: Employs action-oriented line-by-line coding using gerunds ('-ing' verbs, e.g., 'navigating bureaucracy', 'protecting self-esteem') to preserve fluidity, agency, and ongoing process.
2. Focused Coding: Elevates the most frequent, significant, or conceptually revealing initial codes to synthesize large swaths of data into higher-order categories.
3. Theoretical Memo-Writing: Continuous, unconstrained, spontaneous memo-writing used as an exploratory space to interrogate categories, discover linkages, and deconstruct researcher assumptions.
4. Reflexive Positionality: Transparently examining how the researcher's background, emotions, and theoretical baggage shape the questions asked and the themes noticed.
5. Theoretical Sampling and Saturation: Gathering additional data to illuminate and define the boundaries, properties, and variations of emergent theoretical categories.
terms.benchmarks:
Methodological criteria (Charmaz, 2006, 2014):
- Four Quality Criteria: Credibility (sufficient depth and data intimacy), Originality (novel categories and fresh conceptual insights), Resonance (meaningful to participants and readers), and Usefulness (actionable in everyday life or policy).
- Action-Oriented Language: Codebooks must emphasize active human agency, process, and meaning rather than static diagnostic labels.
- Deep Reflexive Disclosures: Manuscripts require transparent reflections on power dynamics, co-construction moments, and ethical dilemmas.
terms.pitfalls:
Common research design flaws in Charmazian studies:
1. Relapsing into Objectivist Terminology: Adopting Charmaz's name but using the rigid, formulaic axial coding paradigms and mechanistic conditional matrices of Strauss and Corbin (1990).
2. Passive Static Coding: Writing passive, noun-heavy codes ('Hospital Policies', 'Employee Stress') instead of dynamic gerunds ('Resisting managerial surveillance').
3. Confusing Grounded Theory with Thematic Analysis: Conducting coding without constant comparison, theoretical memoing, or theoretical sampling, yielding mere thematic description rather than an integrated explanatory theory.
terms.apa_reference: Charmaz, K. (2014). Constructing grounded theory (2nd ed.). SAGE Publications.

terms.core_definition: A Constructivist Worldview—synthesized as a foundational research framework by John W. Creswell (2014) alongside Postpositivism, Transformative, and Pragmatic worldviews—is a philosophical paradigm that assumes individuals develop subjective, varied, and multiple meanings of their lived experiences directed toward specific objects or things. The goal of research anchored in a constructivist worldview is to rely as much as possible on the participants' views of the situation being studied, using broad, open-ended questions and inductive inquiry to uncover the historical, social, and cultural settings in which individuals live and work.
terms.seminal_citation: Creswell, J. W. (2014). Research design: Qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods approaches (4th ed.). SAGE Publications.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Constructivist worldview according to Creswell & Creswell (2023).
terms.operational_mechanism:
Operating under a constructivist worldview requires four research design principles:
1. Subjective Meaning Elicitation: Posing open-ended, non-leading questions that permit informants to construct their own narratives without being channeled into predefined rating categories.
2. Contextual Immersion: Recognizing that human experiences are formed through interaction with others and historical/cultural norms; researchers immerse themselves in the participants' actual social environment.
3. Inductive Theory Generation: Rather than beginning with a formal theory to test deductively, the investigator generates or inductively develops a theory or pattern of meaning throughout the research process.
4. Transparent Reflexivity: The researcher explicitly positions themselves within the inquiry, acknowledging that their own personal, cultural, and historical background shapes their interpretation of the data.
terms.benchmarks:
Research design benchmarks (Creswell, 2014; Crotty, 1998):
- Research Question Alignment: Primary research questions must begin with exploratory, non-directional stems ('How do...', 'What does... mean to...').
- Inductive Logic Flow: Visual representation showing movement from specific raw narrative data, through codes and broader categories, to an overarching theoretical model or pattern.
- Participant Voice Primacy: Generous use of extended verbatim participant quotes to ground all analytical claims.
terms.pitfalls:
Common research design inconsistencies:
1. Paradigm Clashing: Declaring a constructivist worldview in Chapter 1, but utilizing closed-ended survey questionnaires and testing directional null hypotheses in Chapter 3.
2. Presuming Objective Detachment: Claiming that the researcher had 'zero influence on the data collection and remained 100% objective', which directly contradicts constructivist philosophy.
3. Over-Simplifying Cultural Context: Treating individual interview responses as isolated psychological facts without analyzing the institutional, political, and cultural environments that shaped those views.
terms.apa_reference: Crotty, M. (1998). The foundations of social research: Meaning and perspective in the research process. SAGE Publications.

terms.vietnamese: Khái niệm cấu trúc trong lý thuyết khoa học
vietnamese_variants: Khái niệm trừu tượng lý thuyết
terms.core_definition: Constructs in Scientific Theory—formally distinguished from intervening variables by Kenneth MacCorquodale and Paul E. Meehl (1948) and systematized in psychometrics by Jum C. Nunnally (1978)—are deliberately formulated, unobservable, abstract conceptual entities invented by scientists to represent systemic phenomena, psychological traits, or organizational capabilities (e.g., Intelligence, Absorptive Capacity, Psychological Safety, Corporate Culture). Unlike concrete, directly observable physical variables (e.g., height, temperature, factory floor square footage), constructs possess conceptual meaning within a broader nomological network of theoretical relations and must be operationalized through measurable empirical indicators.
terms.seminal_citation: MacCorquodale, K., & Meehl, P. E. (1948). On a distinction between hypothetical constructs and intervening variables. Psychological Review, 55(2), 95-107. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0056029
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Constructs according to Creswell & Creswell (2023).
terms.operational_mechanism:
The scientific formulation and validation of constructs operate across four stages:
1. Theoretical Explication: Formulating an explicit, non-tautological conceptual definition that delineates the construct's core properties, dimensionality, and boundary conditions.
2. Operationalization: Selecting or developing concrete observable indicators (survey items, behavioral metrics, physiological signals) hypothesized to reflect or form the construct.
3. Nomological Network Placement (Cronbach & Meehl): Specifying theoretical propositions that link the focal construct to antecedent, mediating, and outcome constructs.
4. Measurement Model Testing: Employing factor analysis or structural equation modeling to verify whether empirical covariances across indicators correspond to theoretical expectations.
terms.benchmarks:
Scientific rigor criteria (MacCorquodale & Meehl, 1948; Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994):
- Surplus Meaning: True hypothetical constructs possess 'surplus meaning' beyond their specific operational definitions—meaning the construct cannot be completely reduced to any single operational test.
- Multidimensional vs. Unidimensional: Clearly distinguishing whether the construct is a single overarching latent trait or a multidimensional construct composed of distinct, correlated sub-dimensions.
- Falsifiability: Constructs must be embedded in testable structural models that allow their existence and causal properties to be empirically challenged.
terms.pitfalls:
Common conceptual errors in scientific submissions:
1. The Reification Fallacy: Treating an abstract hypothetical construct as if it were a physical, tangible material object existing inside the brain or firm, rather than a scientific conceptual model.
2. Operationism / Operational Reductions: Defining a construct purely as 'what the test measures' (e.g., 'Intelligence is whatever the IQ test scores'), which strips the construct of its theoretical explanatory power.
3. The Jangle Fallacy: Inventing a 'brand new construct' with flashy corporate jargon that is conceptually and empirically identical to a long-established construct (e.g., repackaging 'Job Satisfaction' as 'Workplace Flourishing').
terms.apa_reference: Nunnally, J. C., & Bernstein, I. H. (1994). Psychometric theory (3rd ed.). McGraw-Hill.

terms.vietnamese: Chỉ số hiệu lực nội dung (CVI: I-CVI và S-CVI)
vietnamese_variants: Chỉ số giá trị nội dung CVI
Độ giá trị nội dung I-CVI và S-CVI
terms.core_definition: The Content Validity Index (CVI)—pioneered by Marion R. Lynn (1986) and standardized by Denise F. Polit and Cheryl Tatano Beck (2006)—is the most widely employed quantitative metric for evaluating the content validity of newly developed scales and clinical questionnaires. Evaluated by a panel of independent content experts rating items on a 4-point ordinal relevance scale, CVI is computed at both the individual item level (Item-level CVI, I-CVI) and the overall scale level (Scale-level CVI, S-CVI), providing an auditable, statistical gatekeeping threshold for item retention, revision, or pruning.
terms.seminal_citation: Lynn, M. R. (1986). Determination and quantification of content validity. Nursing Research, 35(6), 382-385. https://doi.org/10.1097/00006199-198611000-00017
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Content Validity Index (CVI - I-CVI & S-CVI) according to Polit & Beck (2006).
terms.operational_mechanism:
The computational and rating protocol operates as follows:
1. Expert Rating Administration: A panel of $N$ content experts (typically 5 to 10 experts) independently rates each item on a 4-point Likert scale: 1 = Not relevant, 2 = Somewhat relevant, 3 = Quite relevant, 4 = Highly relevant.
2. Item-Level CVI (I-CVI): For each item, I-CVI is the proportion of experts who rate the item as relevant (giving a score of 3 or 4):
$$\text{I-CVI} = \frac{N_{\text{agree (3 or 4)}}}{N_{\text{total experts}}}$$
3. Scale-Level CVI (S-CVI):
   - Universal Agreement Method (S-CVI/UA): The proportion of items on the scale that achieved unanimous agreement (rated 3 or 4 by *all* experts).
   - Average Method (S-CVI/Ave): The arithmetic mean of all I-CVIs across the entire instrument (the preferred gold standard):
$$\text{S-CVI/Ave} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \text{I-CVI}_i}{k}$$
4. Modified Kappa ($\kappa^*$): Computes chance-adjusted agreement (Polit et al., 2007) to ensure high I-CVI is not an artifact of random chance agreement.
terms.benchmarks:
Established psychometric thresholds (Lynn, 1986; Polit & Beck, 2006):
- Minimum Panel Size: Minimum 3 experts; optimal panel is 6 to 10 qualified experts.
- I-CVI Cutoff: For a panel of 6 to 10 experts, $\text{I-CVI} \ge 0.78$ is mandatory for item retention (for 5 or fewer experts, unanimous agreement $\text{I-CVI} = 1.00$ is required).
- S-CVI/Ave Cutoff: Overall scale $\text{S-CVI/Ave} \ge 0.90$ indicates excellent content validity (minimum acceptable: $0.80$).
- Modified Kappa ($\kappa^*$): $\kappa^* \ge 0.74$ indicates excellent chance-adjusted agreement; $0.60 \le \kappa^* < 0.74$ is good.
terms.pitfalls:
Common methodological traps in scale validation:
1. Using a 3-Point or 5-Point Scale with Neutral Midpoint: Using an odd-numbered scale allows experts to choose a non-committal neutral option ('Ambivalent'), destroying the binary relevance calculation (a 4-point scale forcing a choice is mandatory).
2. Reporting Only S-CVI/UA: Reporting only universal agreement S-CVI/UA; as scale length increases to 30 items, achieving unanimous agreement across all experts on every item becomes virtually impossible, making S-CVI/UA overly conservative.
3. Using Non-Expert Convenience Panels: Recruiting graduate students or casual peers rather than true clinical or theoretical domain experts, producing invalid content validity ratings.
terms.apa_reference: Polit, D. F., & Beck, C. T. (2006). The content validity index: Are you sure you know what's being reported? Critique and recommendations. Research in Nursing & Health, 29(5), 489-497. https://doi.org/10.1002/nur.20147

terms.term: Content Validity Index (CVI - I-CVI & S-CVI Framework)
terms.vietnamese: Chỉ số giá trị nội dung (I-CVI & S-CVI - Lynn / Polit & Beck)
vietnamese_variants: Định lượng giá trị nội dung
terms.core_definition: Content Validity Index (CVI) là phương pháp định lượng phổ biến và được thừa nhận rộng rãi nhất trên thế giới để đánh giá giá trị nội dung của một công cụ đo lường dựa trên phán đoán của hội đồng chuyên gia độc lập (Lynn, 1986; Polit & Beck, 2006). CVI chia thành 2 cấp độ: (1) I-CVI (Item-level CVI) - tỷ lệ chuyên gia đánh giá một câu hỏi cụ thể là phù hợp/cần thiết; (2) S-CVI (Scale-level CVI) - mức độ phù hợp nội dung của toàn bộ thang đo.
terms.seminal_citation: Lynn, M. R. (1986). Determination and quantification of content validity. Nursing Research, 35(6), 382-385; Polit, D. F., & Beck, C. T. (2006). The content validity index: Are you sure you know what's being reported? Research in Nursing & Health, 29(5), 489-497.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Content Validity Index (CVI) according to Polit & Beck (2006).
benchmarks: Ngưỡng I-CVI tối thiểu: Nếu hội đồng có 3-5 chuyên gia, I-CVI phải đạt 1.00; Nếu hội đồng có từ 6 chuyên gia trở lên, I-CVI >= 0.78 (Lynn, 1986; Polit & Beck, 2006).
Ngưỡng S-CVI/Ave tối thiểu: Toàn bộ thang đo phải đạt S-CVI/Ave >= 0.90 để được coi là có giá trị nội dung xuất sắc.
Quy mô hội đồng: Tối thiểu 5 chuyên gia và lý tưởng từ 6 đến 10 chuyên gia có uy tín học thuật hoặc thực tiễn sâu.
pitfalls: Sử dụng thang đo 5 điểm có điểm trung tính: Điểm trung tính (mức 3) làm loãng sự phán đoán, bắt buộc phải dùng thang 4 điểm để chuyên gia buộc phải đưa ra lập trường.
Chỉ báo cáo S-CVI/Ave mà giấu I-CVI: Lấy trung bình cao để che giấu những câu hỏi có I-CVI cực thấp (< 0.60) cần phải loại bỏ.
Chuyên gia không độc lập hoặc không đủ tiêu chuẩn: Mời bạn bè, đồng nghiệp cùng phòng làm chuyên gia thẩm định dẫn đến kết quả CVI bị thổi phồng giả tạo.
terms.operational_mechanism: Quy trình thực thi: (1) Hội đồng chuyên gia (thường từ 5 đến 10 người) chấm điểm từng câu hỏi trên thang đo Likert 4 mức độ: 1 = Không phù hợp, 2 = Cần chỉnh sửa nhiều, 3 = Phù hợp nhưng cần chỉnh sửa nhỏ, 4 = Hoàn toàn phù hợp; (2) I-CVI = (Số chuyên gia cho điểm 3 hoặc 4) / (Tổng số chuyên gia); (3) S-CVI tính theo 2 cách: S-CVI/UA (Universal Agreement - tỷ lệ câu hỏi đạt 100% chuyên gia đồng thuận) hoặc S-CVI/Ave (Trung bình cộng của tất cả các I-CVI trong thang đo).
terms.apa_reference: Polit, D. F., & Beck, C. T. (2006). The content validity index: Are you sure you know what's being reported? Critique and recommendations. Research in Nursing & Health, 29(5), 489-497. https://doi.org/10.1002/nur.20147

terms.vietnamese: Tỷ lệ hiệu lực nội dung (CVR - Lawshe)
vietnamese_variants: Tỷ lệ giá trị nội dung Lawshe
terms.core_definition: The Content Validity Ratio (CVR) is a classic quantitative statistical technique developed by C. H. Lawshe (1975) to establish the content validity of job-knowledge tests, psychological instruments, and employee selection batteries. Administered to a panel of subject matter experts (SMEs) who evaluate whether each proposed item is 'essential,' 'useful but not essential,' or 'not necessary' to the performance of a construct or job role, CVR measures the degree to which expert consensus that an item is 'essential' exceeds chance expectations.
terms.seminal_citation: Lawshe, C. H. (1975). A quantitative approach to content validity. Personnel Psychology, 28(4), 563-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1744-6570.1975.tb01393.x
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Content Validity Ratio (CVR - Lawshe) according to Lawshe (1975).
terms.operational_mechanism:
The mathematical formulation and decision rule are defined as follows:
1. SME Rating Categorization: Each expert on a panel of $N$ subject matter experts assigns each item to one of three categories: (1) Essential, (2) Useful but not essential, (3) Not necessary.
2. Lawshe's CVR Formula:
$$\text{CVR} = \frac{n_e - \frac{N}{2}}{\frac{N}{2}} = \frac{2n_e - N}{N}$$
where $n_e$ is the number of panelists rating the item as 'essential', and $N$ is total panel size.
3. Value Range: CVR ranges from $-1.0$ (when no experts rate it essential) to $0.0$ (when exactly half rate it essential) to $+1.0$ (when all experts rate it essential).
4. Content Validity Index (CVI - Lawshe's overall index): The average of CVR values across all retained items:
$$\text{CVI} = \frac{\sum \text{CVR}}{\text{Total retained items}}$$
terms.benchmarks:
Lawshe's critical cutoff thresholds (one-tailed $\alpha = 0.05$, Wilson et al., 2012):
- Panel of 5 experts: Minimum $\text{CVR} = 0.99$ (unanimous agreement required).
- Panel of 8 experts: Minimum $\text{CVR} = 0.75$.
- Panel of 10 experts: Minimum $\text{CVR} = 0.62$.
- Panel of 15 experts: Minimum $\text{CVR} = 0.49$.
- Panel of 20 experts: Minimum $\text{CVR} = 0.42$.
- Decision Rule: Any item whose CVR fails to meet the critical threshold for that specific panel size is statistically indistinguishable from chance and must be eliminated.
terms.pitfalls:
Common research reporting errors:
1. Using Lawshe's Original Flawed Table: Citing Lawshe's 1975 original published threshold table, which contained computational errors in small-sample normal approximations; researchers should use the corrected binomial critical values published by Wilson et al. (2012).
2. Arbitrary Threshold Setting: Using an arbitrary cutoff (e.g., 'all items with CVR $> 0.50$ were kept') without adjusting for the specific panel size $N$.
3. Confusing Lawshe's CVI with Lynn's CVI: Conflating Lawshe's Content Validity Index (mean CVR) with Lynn's (1986) Scale-level Content Validity Index (S-CVI/Ave).
terms.apa_reference: Wilson, F. R., Pan, W., & Schumsky, D. A. (2012). Recalculation of the critical values for Lawshe's content validity ratio. Measurement and Evaluation in Counseling and Development, 45(3), 197-210. https://doi.org/10.1177/0748175612440286

terms.vietnamese: Tỷ số giá trị nội dung CVR (Phương pháp C. H. Lawshe)
vietnamese_variants: Định lượng giá trị nội dung Lawshe
terms.core_definition: Content Validity Ratio (CVR) là phương pháp thống kê đầu tiên trong lịch sử tâm lý học đo lường dùng để định lượng hóa mức độ đồng thuận của hội đồng chuyên gia về sự cần thiết của một câu hỏi đo lường, do C. H. Lawshe sáng lập (1975). Phương pháp này kiểm định xem số lượng chuyên gia khẳng định một câu hỏi là 'thiết yếu' (essential) có vượt trội hơn hẳn so với mức độ trùng hợp ngẫu nhiên theo phân phối xác suất nhị thức hay không.
terms.seminal_citation: Lawshe, C. H. (1975). A quantitative approach to content validity. Personnel Psychology, 28(4), 563-575; Ayre, C., & Scally, A. J. (2014). Critical values for Lawshe's content validity ratio: Revisiting the original methods of calculation. Measurement and Evaluation in Counseling and Development, 47(1), 79-86.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Content Validity Ratio (CVR) according to Lawshe (1975).
terms.operational_mechanism: Công thức toán học của Lawshe: CVR = (n_e - N/2) / (N/2), trong đó n_e là số lượng chuyên gia đánh giá câu hỏi là 'Thiết yếu' (Essential), và N là tổng số chuyên gia trong ban hội đồng. Giá trị CVR dao động từ -1.0 (toàn bộ chuyên gia coi là không cần thiết) đến +1.0 (toàn bộ chuyên gia coi là thiết yếu). Sau khi tinh lọc các biến đạt CVR, Chỉ số giá trị nội dung toàn bài (Content Validity Index - CVI theo Lawshe) được tính bằng trung bình cộng các giá trị CVR của các câu hỏi được giữ lại.
benchmarks: Bảng ngưỡng CVR tới hạn của Lawshe (mức ý nghĩa một đuôi alpha = 0.05): Với N = 5 chuyên gia, CVR_min = 0.99; Với N = 6, CVR_min = 0.99; Với N = 8, CVR_min = 0.75; Với N = 10, CVR_min = 0.62; Với N = 14, CVR_min = 0.51; Với N = 20, CVR_min = 0.42 (đã được hiệu chỉnh chính xác bởi Ayre & Scally, 2014).
Quy tắc loại trừ: Bất kỳ câu hỏi nào có giá trị CVR thực tế nhỏ hơn giá trị CVR tới hạn tương ứng với quy mô ban hội đồng đều bắt buộc phải bị loại bỏ.
Định dạng đánh giá 3 mức: (1) Thiết yếu (Essential); (2) Hữu ích nhưng không thiết yếu; (3) Không cần thiết.
pitfalls: Sử dụng bảng giá trị tới hạn cũ có sai số toán học: Bảng nguyên bản năm 1975 của Lawshe có một số sai số làm tròn xác suất, nên sử dụng bảng hiệu chỉnh chính xác của Ayre & Scally (2014).
Nhầm lẫn giữa CVR của Lawshe và CVI của Lynn: Áp dụng lẫn lộn công thức tính khiến việc đối chiếu ngưỡng tới hạn bị sai lệch.
Ban chuyên gia dưới 5 người: Khi N < 5, công thức CVR không có ý nghĩa thống kê vì không thể bác bỏ giả thuyết ngẫu nhiên.
terms.apa_reference: Lawshe, C. H. (1975). A quantitative approach to content validity. Personnel Psychology, 28(4), 563-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1744-6570.1975.tb01393.x

terms.vietnamese: Tiếp cận liên tục trong nghiên cứu thực địa dài hạn
vietnamese_variants: Duy trì tiếp cận nghiên cứu
Tiếp cận thực địa kéo dài
terms.core_definition: Continuing Access is a critical operational and methodological challenge in organizational ethnography, longitudinal qualitative fieldwork, and multi-wave case studies, analyzed by Mark Saunders, Philip Lewis, and Adrian Thornhill (2019). It refers to the researcher's ongoing ability to sustain, nurture, and renegotiate physical, cognitive, and political access to an organization, elite executives, or field informants over extended temporal windows (months or years). Unlike initial access (securing gatekeeper consent for a single visit), continuing access is fragile, constantly threatened by corporate restructuring, executive turnover, participant fatigue, changing political climates, or emergent organizational crises.
terms.seminal_citation: Saunders, M. N. K., Lewis, P., & Thornhill, A. (2019). Research methods for business students (8th ed.). Pearson Education.
terms.expert_notes: Đã được biên tập và chuẩn hóa định nghĩa học thuật theo giáo trình kinh điển.
terms.core_definition_en: Rigorous scholarly definition of Continuing access according to established research methodology literature.
terms.operational_mechanism:
Managing continuing access requires four relational and operational strategies:
1. Incremental Renegotiation: Treating organizational access not as a one-time transactional contract, but as an ongoing relational negotiation at every data collection phase.
2. Champion Cultivation and Redundancy: Developing relationships with multiple internal sponsors and informal champions, ensuring that if a key sponsor departs or is promoted, access does not instantly collapse.
3. Reciprocal Value Delivery: Providing non-confidential, actionable interim executive summaries, workshops, or methodological briefings that demonstrate tangible value to the host organization without compromising research neutrality.
4. Boundary and Ethical Sensitivity: Demonstrating acute sensitivity to organizational stress periods (quarterly earnings, audits, layoffs), pausing fieldwork to protect participant goodwill.
terms.benchmarks:
Fieldwork quality criteria (Saunders et al., 2019; Feldman et al., 2003):
- Panel Retention in Longitudinal Qualitative Studies: Documenting attrition rates across interview waves and demonstrating how continued access was preserved.
- Ethical Drift Prevention: Ensuring that extended immersion does not lead to 'going native' or informal compromises of participant confidentiality.
- Trust Milestones: Informants continuing to grant backstage observations and disclosing sensitive internal developments during subsequent waves.
terms.pitfalls:
Common fieldwork hazards leading to research termination:
1. The 'Single Point of Failure' Dependency: Relying exclusively on one high-ranking executive for access; when that executive leaves the firm, the researcher is permanently barred by their successor.
2. Over-Demanding Informant Burden: Scheduling intrusive 2-hour interviews during critical operational crunches, burning out participant goodwill.
3. Breaching Informal Trust: Leaking sensitive remarks made by lower-level employees to management during interim updates, instantly destroying continuing access across the workforce.
terms.apa_reference: Feldman, M. S., Bell, J., & Berger, M. T. (2003). Gaining access: A practical and theoretical guide for qualitative researchers. Rowman Altamira.

terms.vietnamese: Thang đo liên tục (Thang đo khoảng và tỷ lệ)
vietnamese_variants: Thang đo khoảng và tỷ lệ
terms.core_definition:
Thang đo liên tục (Continuous Scales / Metric Quantitative Scales, được định hình bởi Stanley Smith Stevens năm 1946) đại diện cho hai cấp độ đo lường cao cấp nhất và hoàn thiện nhất trong khoa học: Thang đo Khoảng (Interval Scale) và Thang đo Tỷ lệ (Ratio Scale). Các thuộc tính đo lường bằng thang đo liên tục về mặt lý thuyết có thể nhận vô số giá trị thực trong một khoảng xác định:
1. Thang đo Khoảng (Interval Scale): Sở hữu thuộc tính phân loại, thứ bậc và khoảng cách đơn vị bằng nhau tuyệt đối giữa các nấc đo lường ($d = x_i - x_j$). Tuy nhiên, thang đo khoảng KHÔNG có điểm gốc không tuyệt đối (Arbitrary Zero Point) — điểm 0 chỉ là một quy ước đo lường chứ không đồng nghĩa với sự vắng mặt hoàn toàn của thuộc tính (ví dụ: Nhiệt độ độ Celsius hay độ Fahrenheit, Điểm số IQ, Điểm số SAT). Phép cộng và trừ có ý nghĩa, nhưng phép nhân và chia tỷ số là vô nghĩa (không thể nói $40^\circ\text{C}$ nóng gấp đôi $20^\circ\text{C}$).
2. Thang đo Tỷ lệ (Ratio Scale): Là đỉnh cao của đo lường, kế thừa toàn bộ tính chất của thang khoảng đồng thời sở hữu Điểm gốc không thực sự (Absolute / True Zero Point) biểu thị sự vắng bóng hoàn toàn của đại lượng đo lường (ví dụ: Thu nhập, Chiều dài, Cân nặng, Doanh thu, Lợi nhuận, Thời gian phản ứng). Mọi phép toán cộng, trừ, nhân, chia đều giữ nguyên ý nghĩa đại số hoàn hảo.
terms.seminal_citation: Stevens, S. S. (1946). On the theory of scales of measurement. Science, 103(2684), 677-680.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Continuous scales according to Creswell & Creswell (2023).
terms.short_definition: Các thang đo định lượng đo lường các thuộc tính liên tục, bao gồm thang đo khoảng (Interval) và thang đo tỷ lệ (Ratio), cho phép thực hiện toàn bộ các phép toán số học.
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Đo lường và thu thập dữ liệu liên tục: Ghi nhận dữ liệu bằng các công cụ đo lường vật lý chính xác hoặc bảng hỏi liên tục (như VAS $100\text{ mm}$ hay tổng hợp điểm composite scores của thang đo đa mục Likert).
2. Thống kê mô tả toàn diện: Được phép tính toán đầy đủ toàn bộ các chỉ số thống kê mô tả tham số: Trung bình cộng (Mean), Phương sai (Variance), Độ lệch chuẩn (Standard Deviation), Hệ số biến thiên (Coefficient of Variation - chỉ áp dụng cho thang tỷ lệ), Độ lệch (Skewness) và Độ nhọn (Kurtosis).
3. Kiểm tra tiền giả định phân phối chuẩn (Normality Testing):
   Áp dụng kiểm định Shapiro-Wilk hoặc Kolmogorov-Smirnov kết hợp trực quan hóa biểu đồ Q-Q Plot.
4. Thực hiện các kỹ thuật thống kê tham số mạnh mẽ (Parametric Statistics):
   Ước lượng Hồi quy tuyến tính bội OLS, Mô hình phương trình cấu trúc (SEM), Phân tích phương sai ANOVA/MANOVA, Phân tích chuỗi thời gian ARIMA.
5. Xử lý vi phạm phân phối: Áp dụng các phép biến đổi dữ liệu (Logarithmic, Box-Cox transformation) hoặc sử dụng các ước lượng vững (Robust standard errors / Huber-White).
terms.benchmarks:
1. Khảo sát phân phối chuẩn: Giá trị tuyệt đối của Skewness $< 2$ và Kurtosis $< 7$ được coi là chấp nhận được để chạy các kỹ thuật tham số theo Kline (2015).
2. Tính khả thi của phép toán tỷ lệ: Chỉ được phép tính tỷ số phần trăm thay đổi ($\Delta \%$) và trung bình nhân (Geometric Mean) đối với dữ liệu thuộc Thang đo Tỷ lệ có gốc 0 thực sự.
3. Độ chính xác đo lường: Đòi hỏi sai số chuẩn đo lường (Standard Error of Measurement - SEM) phải được báo cáo kèm theo khoảng tin cậy của ước lượng.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Tính toán tỷ lệ phần trăm trên Thang đo Khoảng: Tuyên bố rằng 'nhiệt độ hôm nay nóng hơn hôm qua $50\%$' khi đo bằng độ Celsius là sai lầm căn bản về bản chất thang đo, vì nếu đổi sang độ Fahrenheit hoặc Kelvin, tỷ lệ phần trăm đó sẽ thay đổi hoàn toàn.
2. Xem nhẹ sự hiện diện của giá trị ngoại lai cực trị (Extreme Outliers): Do thang đo liên tục sử dụng trung bình cộng và phương sai, các giá trị dị biệt cực lớn có thể làm biến dạng hoàn toàn đường hồi quy OLS.
3. Ép buộc dữ liệu bị chặn biên vào mô hình liên tục thông thường: Khi biến liên tục bị chặn dưới tại 0 (như chi phí y tế, doanh số bán hàng có nhiều ca bằng 0), áp dụng OLS sẽ dẫn đến dự báo giá trị âm phi thực tế; bắt buộc phải sử dụng mô hình Tobit hoặc mô hình hai phần (Two-part models).
terms.apa_reference: Stevens, S. S. (1946). On the theory of scales of measurement. Science, 103(2684), 677-680. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.103.2684.677

terms.core_definition: A Contour-Enhanced Funnel Plot is an advanced diagnostic meta-analytic graphical technique, developed by Jaime L. Peters et al. (2008), that enhances standard funnel plots by overlaying shaded contours representing specific statistical significance regions (e.g., $p < 0.01$, $p < 0.05$, $p < 0.10$, and $p > 0.10$). In classical funnel plots, asymmetry is traditionally attributed to publication bias; however, asymmetry can also arise from true study heterogeneity, variable intervention intensity, or small-study artifacts. By displaying where missing studies fall relative to statistical significance thresholds, the contour-enhanced funnel plot allows researchers to differentiate genuine publication bias (studies missing specifically in the non-significant white region) from other structural causes of asymmetry.
terms.seminal_citation: Peters, J. L., Sutton, A. J., Jones, D. R., Abrams, K. R., & Rushton, L. (2008). Contour-enhanced meta-analysis funnel plots help distinguish publication bias from other causes of asymmetry. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 61(10), 991-996. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2007.11.010
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Contour-Enhanced Funnel Plot according to Peters et al. (2008).
terms.operational_mechanism:
The graphical and analytical construction functions as follows:
1. Standard Plot Layout: Scatter plot of individual study effect sizes (horizontal axis) against precision or standard error (vertical axis, inverted so larger, more precise studies appear at the top).
2. Superimposed Significance Contours: Shaded regions represent critical values of the test statistic ($z$-values of $1.64, 1.96, 2.58$):
   - Dark gray / colored bands indicate regions of statistical significance ($p < 0.01$, $p < 0.05$, $p < 0.10$).
   - The central unshaded / white region indicates non-significance ($p > 0.10$).
3. Diagnostic Rule for Publication Bias:
   - If the funnel plot is asymmetric and the 'missing' small studies fall predominantly in the central non-significant region ($p > 0.10$), publication bias is the primary plausible cause (editors and authors suppressed non-significant findings).
   - If the 'missing' studies fall in regions of statistical significance, or if small studies cluster in areas of significance despite conflicting effect directions, asymmetry is driven by clinical heterogeneity, methodological diversity, or small-study biases rather than suppression of non-significant results.
terms.benchmarks:
Meta-analysis reporting standards (Peters et al., 2008; Higgins et al., 2023 - Cochrane Handbook):
- Standard Tool in R & Stata: Readily implemented via `metafor::funnel(..., contour = c(0.9, 0.95, 0.99))` in R or `confunnel` in Stata.
- Minimum Study Requirement: Recommended when meta-analyses contain at least 10 or more studies ($k \ge 10$); with fewer studies, visual funnel inspection has negligible diagnostic power.
- Dual Reporting: High-impact systematic reviews present contour-enhanced funnel plots alongside quantitative asymmetry tests (Egger's regression test, Begg's rank test).
terms.pitfalls:
Common interpretation errors in meta-analyses:
1. Automatic Assumption of Publication Bias: Treating any funnel asymmetry as definitive proof of publication bias without inspecting the contour zones.
2. Subjective Asymmetry Interpretation in Small Meta-Analyses: Visualizing funnel plots when $k = 5$ or $6$, where random sampling variation naturally creates visual asymmetry.
3. Inappropriate Choice of Precision Metric: Plotting sample size ($N$) on the vertical axis instead of standard error ($	ext{SE}$) or variance ($1/	ext{SE}^2$), which distorts the theoretical triangular funnel boundaries.
terms.apa_reference: Higgins, J. P. T., Thomas, J., Chandler, J., Cumpston, M., Li, T., Page, M. J., & Welch, V. A. (Eds.). (2023). Cochrane handbook for systematic reviews of interventions (Version 6.4). The Cochrane Collaboration.

terms.vietnamese: Phân loại vai trò đóng góp tác giả (CRediT)
vietnamese_variants: Chuẩn phân loại tác giả CRediT
Hệ thống phân loại đóng góp CRediT
terms.core_definition: The Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) is an internationally standardized, 14-role metadata taxonomy created by Amy Brand, Liz Allen, and colleagues (2015; formalized as ANSI/NISO Z39.104-2022) to provide transparent, unambiguous, and granular recognition of each author's specific intellectual, operational, and managerial contributions to a scientific publication. Endorsed by major publishers (Elsevier, Springer Nature, Wiley, PLOS), CRediT dismantles the ambiguous traditional authorship order, combats ghost authorship and honorary/guest authorship, and ensures that diverse contributions (such as software coding, data curation, project administration, and formal analysis) are formally credited.
terms.seminal_citation: Brand, A., Allen, L., Altman, M., Hlava, M., & Scott, J. (2015). Beyond authorship: Attribution, contribution, collaboration, and credit. Learned Publishing, 28(2), 151-155. https://doi.org/10.1087/20150211
terms.expert_notes: Định nghĩa và ngưỡng kiểm định chuẩn hóa từ Cơ sở dữ liệu Viết tắt Học thuật (Acronym Registry).
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Contributor Roles Taxonomy according to Bắt buộc khai báo tại các nhà xuất bản hàng đầu (Elsevier, Springer Nature, Wiley, PLOS) nhằm xóa bỏ tình trạng 'tác giả danh dự' (gift authorship)..
terms.benchmarks:
Publishing standards (Brand et al., 2015; Allen et al., 2019; NISO standard):
- Granular Attribution: Each co-author must be assigned one or more specific roles; roles can be designated as 'Lead', 'Equal', or 'Supporting'.
- Published Declarations: High-impact journals mandate a dedicated 'Author Contributions' section formatted explicitly using CRediT role syntax.
- ICMJE Harmony: An individual must still meet the foundational ICMJE authorship criteria (approving final draft, accountability) to be listed as a co-author with CRediT roles; non-author contributors are listed in Acknowledgments.
terms.operational_mechanism:
The CRediT system classifies authorship across 14 standardized, non-overlapping roles:
1. Conceptualization: Ideas; formulation of overarching research goals.
2. Data Curation: Management activities to annotate, scrub, and maintain research data.
3. Formal Analysis: Application of statistical, mathematical, or computational techniques to analyze study data.
4. Funding Acquisition: Acquisition of financial support for the project.
5. Investigation: Conducting the research experiments or data collection.
6. Methodology: Development or design of methodology; creation of models.
7. Project Administration: Management and coordination responsibility for the research activity planning and execution.
8. Resources: Provision of study materials, patients, laboratory samples, instrumentation, or computing resources.
9. Software: Programming, software development, designing computer programs, and testing code.
10. Supervision: Oversight and leadership responsibility for research execution.
11. Validation: Verification of the overall replication/reproducibility of results.
12. Visualization: Preparation and creation of published figures, charts, and presentations.
13. Writing – Original Draft: Preparation, creation, and presentation of the initial published work.
14. Writing – Review & Editing: Critical review, commentary, or revision by research group members.
terms.pitfalls:
Common research ethics traps in authorship management:
1. Honorary / Gift Authorship Masking: Assigning nominal CRediT roles (e.g., 'Supervision' or 'Resources') to senior department chairs who had zero intellectual contact with the study, violating research integrity.
2. Ghostwriting Concealment: Omitting junior researchers or professional statisticians who performed the entire 'Formal Analysis' or 'Investigation' from the CRediT statement.
3. Inconsistent Multi-Author Declarations: Submitting a paper where nobody is credited with 'Conceptualization' or 'Writing – Original Draft', signaling an unethical submission process.
terms.apa_reference: Allen, L., O'Connell, A., & Kiermer, V. (2019). How can we ensure visibility and diversity in research contributions? How the Contributor Role Taxonomy (CRediT) is helping the shift from authorship to contributorship. Learned Publishing, 32(1), 71-76. https://doi.org/10.1002/leap.1210

terms.vietnamese: Chọn mẫu thuận tiện và các cạm bẫy phương pháp luận
vietnamese_variants: Lấy mẫu ngẫu nhiên tiện lợi
terms.core_definition: Convenience Sampling (Chọn mẫu thuận tiện) là phương pháp chọn mẫu phi xác suất trong đó đối tượng nghiên cứu được tuyển chọn hoàn toàn dựa trên sự sẵn có, vị trí địa lý thuận lợi và mức độ dễ dàng tiếp cận đối với nhà nghiên cứu (Bornstein et al., 2013). Mặc dù tiết kiệm chi phí và thời gian, đây là phương pháp có giá trị khoa học thấp nhất trong nghiên cứu học thuật, dễ gây ra các thiên kiến chọn mẫu nghiêm trọng (selection bias) và thường bị các hội đồng tiến sĩ hoặc tạp chí Q1 bác bỏ nếu tác giả không chứng minh được tính nghiêm cẩn phương pháp luận bổ trợ.
terms.seminal_citation: Bornstein, M. H., Jager, J., & Putnick, D. L. (2013). Sampling in developmental science: Situations, shortcomings, solutions, and standards. Developmental Review, 33(4), 357-394; Etikan, I., Musa, S. A., & Alkassim, R. S. (2016). Comparison of convenience sampling and purposive sampling. American Journal of Theoretical and Applied Statistics, 5(1), 1-4.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Convenience Sampling according to Schindler (2022).
terms.operational_mechanism: Cơ chế vận hành: Lựa chọn những người có mặt ngay tại chỗ (ví dụ: sinh viên trong lớp học, người đi đường, bạn bè trên mạng xã hội). Để hạn chế tối đa khiếm khuyết mang tính bản chất của phương pháp này khi bắt buộc phải sử dụng (ví dụ trong nghiên cứu thí điểm - pilot study), nhà nghiên cứu phải: (1) Đo lường và báo cáo minh bạch đặc điểm nhân khẩu học so với quần thể; (2) Thực hiện phân tích kiểm tra độ nhạy (sensitivity analysis); (3) Tuyên bố rõ ràng các giới hạn nghiên cứu (limitations).
benchmarks: Chỉ nên chấp nhận trong giai đoạn sơ cấp: Thích hợp cho nghiên cứu thử nghiệm công cụ đo lường (pilot test, pre-test bảng hỏi) hoặc các đề tài khám phá ban đầu.
Bắt buộc công bố ma trận thiên kiến (Bias disclosure): Phải so sánh cơ cấu mẫu với các tham số điều tra quốc gia để người đọc nhận biết độ lệch mẫu.
Cấm suy diễn thống kê ra quần thể: Tuyệt đối không sử dụng các kiểm định tham số để suy rộng kết quả ra toàn xã hội.
pitfalls: Ngụy trang chọn mẫu thuận tiện thành chọn mẫu xác suất: Thu thập dữ liệu thuận tiện trên mạng xã hội nhưng viết trong bài báo là 'lấy mẫu ngẫu nhiên đơn giản'.
Thiên kiến người tình nguyện (Volunteer bias): Những người sẵn lòng trả lời thường có thái độ hoặc thời gian rảnh rỗi rất khác biệt so với người bình thường.
Tuyên bố kết quả có giá trị khái quát hóa cao: Đây là lỗi tử huyệt khiến bài báo bị Reject ngay lập tức tại vòng bình duyệt đầu tiên (Desk reject).
terms.apa_reference: Bornstein, M. H., Jager, J., & Putnick, D. L. (2013). Sampling in developmental science: Situations, shortcomings, solutions, and standards. Developmental Review, 33(4), 357-394. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dr.2013.08.003

terms.vietnamese: Thiết kế hội tụ trong phương pháp hỗn hợp
vietnamese_variants: Thiết kế hỗn hợp hội tụ
terms.core_definition: The Convergent Design—codified as one of the three primary core mixed methods designs by John W. Creswell and Vicki L. Plano Clark (2018; historically referred to as the Concurrent Triangulation Design)—is a single-phase mixed methods design wherein the researcher collects and analyzes both quantitative data (numeric, statistical) and qualitative data (textual, thematic) during the same general timeframe, with approximately equal priority. The two distinct datasets are analyzed independently, and the results are then merged (converged) during the interpretation phase through side-by-side comparison tables, joint displays, or data transformation to determine whether the two diverse sources of evidence corroborate, complement, or contradict each other.
terms.seminal_citation: Creswell, J. W., & Plano Clark, V. L. (2018). Designing and conducting mixed methods research (3rd ed.). SAGE Publications.
terms.expert_notes: Rác Markdown/bảng
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Convergent design according to Creswell & Creswell (2023).
terms.operational_mechanism:
The operational workflow functions across four sequential steps:
1. Concurrent Data Collection: Gathering quantitative data (e.g., probability survey sample $N = 500$) and qualitative data (e.g., purposive semi-structured interviews $n = 30$) concurrently to address closely related research questions.
2. Separate Initial Analysis: Analyzing the quantitative database using inferential statistics and analyzing the qualitative database using thematic coding, keeping analyses independent to avoid premature bias.
3. Merging and Point of Interface: Merging the two analytical strands using formal techniques:
   - Side-by-Side Joint Displays: Presenting quantitative statistics alongside corresponding qualitative themes in comparative tables.
   - Data Transformation: Transforming qualitative themes into counts or dummy variables ('quantitizing') to run regression models.
4. Synthesis & Interpretation of Meta-Inferences: Generating meta-inferences that synthesize the findings, explicitly reporting instances of convergence (confirmation), complementarity (expansion), and divergence (discordance).
terms.benchmarks:
Methodological standards (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018; Guetterman et al., 2015):
- Visual Notation: Designated in standard Morse notation as $\text{QUAL} + \text{QUANT}$ (signifying concurrent timing and equal weighting).
- Joint Display Requirement: High-impact publications must include an integrated joint display table that directly juxtaposes quantitative statistical results against qualitative quotes and thematic matrices.
- Sample Alignment: Although sample sizes differ, qualitative and quantitative participants must be drawn from the exact same institutional setting or target population.
terms.pitfalls:
Common reviewer rejection reasons in mixed methods manuscripts:
1. Superficial Integration (The 'Two Studies' Defect): Reporting quantitative findings in Study 1 and qualitative findings in Study 2 without ever merging them in a joint display or generating integrated meta-inferences.
2. Concealing Discordant Findings: When quantitative surveys show positive satisfaction but qualitative interviews reveal deep employee anger, omitting the qualitative contradiction to present a false impression of harmony (divergence must be highlighted as a valuable finding).
3. Asymmetric Rigor: Conducting a rigorous 500-person survey, but pairing it with 3 brief, convenience-sample informal chats, violating qualitative sampling and saturation standards.
terms.apa_reference: Guetterman, T. C., Fetters, M. D., & Creswell, J. W. (2015). Integrating quantitative and qualitative results in health science mixed methods research through joint displays. The Annals of Family Medicine, 13(6), 554-561. https://doi.org/10.1370/afm.1865

terms.vietnamese: Khung phương pháp hỗn hợp hội tụ

terms.core_definition: The Convergent Mixed Methods Framework is an integrative research architecture formulated by John W. Creswell and Vicki L. Plano Clark (2018) that formalizes the collection, separate analysis, and multi-level merging of quantitative and qualitative data within a single empirical study. Emphasizing that numeric and narrative data provide different but equally valuable types of knowledge, this framework operationalizes integration at the analytical and interpretive stages through data transformation, side-by-side joint displays, and multi-dimensional convergence matrices, providing actionable procedures to corroborate findings, expand breadth, and resolve contradictory evidence.
terms.seminal_citation: Creswell, J. W., & Plano Clark, V. L. (2018). Designing and conducting mixed methods research (3rd ed.). SAGE Publications.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Convergent mixed methods according to Creswell & Creswell (2023).
terms.operational_mechanism:
The framework operates through four standardized architectural components:
1. Parallel Independent Strands: Quantitative survey or experimental data and qualitative interview, observational, or textual data are gathered concurrently to answer convergent research questions.
2. Independent Analytical Integrity: Quantitative data are analyzed with inferential statistics (regressions, factor models) and qualitative data are analyzed with rigorous inductive coding, without allowing one strand to contaminate the initial analytical decisions of the other.
3. The Merging Interface: The two independent databases are integrated through:
   - Side-by-Side Joint Displays: Structured tables displaying statistical parameters next to illustrative qualitative quotes and thematic matrices.
   - Data Transformation: 'Quantitizing' qualitative codes into numeric presence/absence indicators or 'qualitizing' demographic profiles into narrative case vignettes.
4. Integrated Meta-Inferences: Deriving overarching meta-inferences that answer the study's central mixed methods research question.
terms.benchmarks:
Design standards (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018; Fetters et al., 2013):
- Strand Priority Declaration: Declaring whether strands carry equal weight ($\text{QUAL} + \text{QUANT}$) or whether one strand is primary.
- Discordance Protocol: Explicitly describing how discrepancies between qualitative and quantitative findings were handled (e.g., collecting follow-up data or re-analyzing outliers).
- Joint Display Complexity: Publishing a multi-column integration display mapping quantitative constructs to qualitative themes and reporting convergence assessments (confirmation, expansion, or discordance).
terms.pitfalls:
Common research design failures:
1. Separate Reporting Silos: Presenting the quantitative results in one isolated section and qualitative findings in another without ever cross-referencing them in the discussion.
2. Discarding Inconvenient Contradictions: Ignoring qualitative findings that directly contradict survey results, missing the most insightful contribution of mixed methods research.
3. Unmatched Sample Contexts: Surveying consumers in one geographic region while conducting qualitative interviews with corporate managers in a completely different country without theoretical rationale.
terms.apa_reference: Fetters, M. D., Curry, L. A., & Creswell, J. W. (2013). Achieving integration in mixed methods designs—principles and practices. Health Services Research, 48(6pt2), 2134-2156. https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-6773.12117

terms.term: Convergent Parallel Mixed Methods Design (QUAN + QUAL)
terms.vietnamese: Thiết kế hỗn hợp song song hội tụ (QUAN + QUAL đồng thời)
vietnamese_variants: Thiết kế đồng thời hội tụ
Mô hình tam giác đạc hỗn hợp song song
terms.core_definition: Convergent Parallel Mixed Methods Design (trước đây gọi là Concurrent Triangulation Design) là thiết kế phương pháp hỗn hợp kinh điển trong đó nhà nghiên cứu tiến hành thu thập và phân tích dữ liệu định lượng (QUAN) và định tính (QUAL) đồng thời trong cùng một khung thời gian với trọng số bình đẳng (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018). Hai cơ sở dữ liệu được phân tích độc lập với nhau, sau đó kết quả được tích hợp (merged) trong giai đoạn diễn giải tổng thể để so sánh trực tiếp, đối chiếu chéo xem các phát hiện định tính và định lượng có hội tụ (converge), bổ sung (complement) hay mâu thuẫn (diverge/contradict) với nhau.
terms.seminal_citation: Creswell, J. W., & Plano Clark, V. L. (2018). Designing and Conducting Mixed Methods Research (3rd ed.). SAGE Publications; Fetters, M. D., Curry, L. A., & Creswell, J. W. (2013). Achieving integration in mixed methods designs—principles and practices. Health Services Research, 48(6pt2), 2134-2156.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Convergent Parallel Design according to Creswell & Plano Clark (2018).
terms.operational_mechanism: Quy trình thực thi 4 bước: (1) Thu thập song song dữ liệu định lượng (khảo sát mẫu lớn) và định tính (phỏng vấn sâu) trên các chủ đề khái niệm tương ứng; (2) Phân tích dữ liệu QUAN bằng thống kê và phân tích dữ liệu QUAL bằng mã hóa chủ đề một cách hoàn toàn độc lập; (3) Tích hợp hai nguồn dữ liệu thông qua Ma trận so sánh bên cạnh (Side-by-side comparison) hoặc Bảng hiển thị liên kết (Joint Display); (4) Thảo luận về các điểm hội tụ và đặc biệt mổ xẻ các mâu thuẫn nhận thức (divergent findings) bằng cách đào sâu dữ liệu mở rộng.
benchmarks: Thiết kế mẫu song song có liên kết: Dù cỡ mẫu khác nhau (QUAN thường N lớn, QUAL N nhỏ), các đối tượng phỏng vấn định tính lý tưởng nhất nên được trích xuất từ chính quần thể nghiên cứu của mẫu khảo sát định lượng.

Sử dụng bảng Joint Display tích hợp: Bắt buộc xuất bản bảng đối chiếu đa cột: Cột 1 (Biến số/Khái niệm) - Cột 2 (Kết quả thống kê định lượng) - Cột 3 (Trích dẫn bằng chứng định tính) - Cột 4 (Đánh giá mức độ hội tụ/bất đồng).
Xử lý nghiêm cẩn các phát hiện mâu thuẫn: Không được che giấu dữ liệu khi định lượng nói 'Có' nhưng định tính nói 'Không'; phải giải thích nguyên nhân gây phân kỳ.
pitfalls: Dùng dữ liệu định tính chỉ để trang trí: Toàn bộ bài báo là phân tích định lượng, chỉ thêm vào 1-2 câu phỏng vấn ngẫu nhiên để minh họa mà gọi là Convergent design.
Thiếu sự tương thích về mặt khái niệm: Bảng câu hỏi định lượng hỏi về khái niệm A, nhưng phỏng vấn định tính lại đi hỏi khái niệm B, khiến việc đối chiếu hội tụ trở nên vô nghĩa.
Bỏ qua phân tích bất đồng dữ liệu (Divergent findings): Khi kết quả hai nhánh mâu thuẫn, nghiên cứu viên vội vã cắt bỏ dữ liệu định tính để bảo vệ mô hình thống kê.
terms.apa_reference: Fetters, M. D., Curry, L. A., & Creswell, J. W. (2013). Achieving integration in mixed methods designs—principles and practices. Health Services Research, 48(6pt2), 2134-2156. https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-6773.12117
